We also support RankGPT and RankGemini variants, which are proprietary listwise rerankers. Addtionally, we support reranking with the first-token logits only to improve inference efficiency. title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces | OpenReview
summary: Foundation models, now powering most of the exciting applications in deep learning, are almost universally based on the Transformer architecture and its core attention module. Many subquadratic-time architectures such as linear attention, gated convolution and recurrent models, and structured state space models (SSMs) have been developed to address Transformers' computational inefficiency on long sequences, but they have not performed as well as attention on important modalities such as language. We identify that a key weakness of such models is their inability to perform content-based reasoning, and make several improvements. First, simply letting the SSM parameters be functions of the input addresses their weakness with discrete modalities, allowing the model to *selectively* propagate or forget information along the sequence length dimension depending on the current token. Second, even though this change prevents the use of efficient convolutions, we design a hardware-aware parallel algorithm in recurrent mode. We integrate these selective SSMs into a simplified end-to-end neural network architecture without attention or even MLP blocks (**Mamba**). Mamba enjoys fast inference (5$\times$ higher throughput than Transformers) and linear scaling in sequence length, and its performance improves on real data up to million-length sequences. As a general sequence model backbone, Mamba achieves state-of-the-art performance across several modalities such as language, audio, and genomics. On language modeling, our Mamba-1.4B model outperforms Transformers of the same size and matches Transformers twice its size, both in pretraining and downstream evaluation.

title: Beyond the Basics of RAG – Parlance
summary: LLMs are powerful, but have limitations: their knowledge is fixed in their weights, and their context window is limited. Worse: when they don’t know something, they might just make it up. RAG, for Retrieval Augmented Generation, has emerged as a way to mitigate both of those problems. However, implementing RAG effectively is more complex than it seems. The nitty gritty parts of what makes good retrieval good are rarely talked about: No, cosine similarity is, in fact, not all you need. In this workshop, we explore what helps build a robust RAG pipeline, and how simple insights from retrieval research can greatly improve your RAG efforts. We’ll cover key topics like BM25, re-ranking, indexing, domain specificity, evaluation beyond LGTM@few, and filtering. Be prepared for a whole new crowd of incredibly useful buzzwords to enter your vocabulary.

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
Love this experiment! Surprised at how well the model followed the output format of reranked_ids, "[8],[3],[2],..." -- I thought that was going to be more difficult!
Reading around DSPy a bit, I think the next step is understanding how Chain of Thought is interfaced with following the output format. Sounds straightforward enough, tweak the output format prompt and then write an example of an explanation followed by output format. 🧠🧩
I hope that gets us past the 75% Recall at 1, if not my next bet would be to add the tool use of retrieving information about the documents to help with re-ranking. Sounds terribly slow for a re-ranker, but maybe this is how we strengthen the explanations to then distill via fine-tuning (with extra points for how small the fine-tuned model can be) 🔥
Quoting @eshorten300
Using GPT-4 to rerank search results 🥸
I want to share two nuggets from my initial experiment:
1. Adding an example of what the output should look like helps the model follow the instructions.
2. Manually tweaking the role description to improve the ranking quality wasn't as straightforward.
The visual shows how to structure a prompt for listwise reranking using OpenAI's API. This includes the role description, output format, and task example.
I tested 4 prompts using 16 @weaviate_io FAQs. This lets you measure recall at 1 because each question has a ground truth answer. The best performing prompt followed the output format 100% of the time (🥳), but only got 75% accuracy across the 16 FAQs. Excited to see how I can improve this with DSPy next! @lateinteraction

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
ラベル数が膨大（>=10k）なとき、テキストの識別をLLMを使ってやろうとすると in-context が長大になり難しいが、
1. テキストからキーとなる表現を抽出（固定LLM）
2. それをもとに類似ラベルを検索（固定Retriever）
3. それをもとにRanking（固定LLM）
というフローを組み、1, 3のFewShot Promptをたった数十個のデータで（GPT-4などの教師LLMを使って）最適化するだけで効率的かつ高精度に識別が実現できるという論文。
医療論文からの薬の副反応の抽出タスク、求人情報からのESCOで定義されたスキルの抽出タスクで実験し、前者ではまだ課題があるが後者ではfine-tuneベースの手法よりも高精度だったとのこと。
実験で行われている通り、タスク的には識別というよりは、表記ゆれのあるテキストからの正規化されたリスト中のアイテムの情報抽出みたいなタスクに向いているのかも。
LLM/Retrieverは所与のもので良く、識別の学習のためのfinetuningは不要。DSPyを使ったコードも非常に短く試しやすそう。
"In-Context Learning for Extreme Multi-Label Classification"
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GEkOM09bMAAOkLC.png
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GEkPjxNaQAA1JoG.jpg

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
i have been exploring the impact of various RAG recipes on retrieval quality and final answers, especially with so many different options available from @langchain alone.
among the numerous choices, i have identified @vespaengine and ColBERT-based retrieval systems as the most promising, particularly when implemented in conjunction with @langchain.
to illustrate, i've compared RAG applied to the same documents using two different recipes:
Recipe#1: @vespaengine's hybrid search + @OpenAI gpt-3.5-turbo + @langchain
Recipe#2: ColBERT + Ragatouille + @trychroma + mixtral-8x7b-instruct-v0.1 + @langchain's EnsembleRetriever

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
It has been shown in various studies that embedding models can perform strong in domain, but have a hard time out-of-domain. Eg in the BEIR paper, DPR was trained on Wikipedia retrieval and is strong there. But on any other dataset it is worse than lexical search.
I also did a quick test for the e5 Mistral model on datasets (robust04, bioasq, signal 1M, TREC news) for which they didn't overfit: Results weren't great, you get the same or better results with 100x smaller (100x cheaper) models.
In-domain performance for embedding models is meaningless if you want to find a good generic Emb model, you always want to evaluate them OOD. By training on all MTEB tasks for these models, the MTEB score for those models become meaningless.

Hello world, DSPy! I am SUPER excited to share a new video walking through the end-to-end of how to use DSPy to optimize the CIFAR-10 for LLM programs, RAG with FAQs! 🛠️
This tutorial contains *4 major parts*: (1) library installation, settings, and creating a dataset with dspy.Example objects, (2) LLM metrics, (3) The DSPy programming model, and (4) Optimization!! 📖
We’ll initialize our RAG prompt off with a very simple `Please answer the question based on the context` prompt, and DSPy then *optimizes* a new description of the task more aligned with the domain of the FAQs, as well as input-output examples from few-shot learning! All guided by the judgement of our LLM metric! 📐
If you’ve ever trained a neural network and had the joy of watching your loss function decrease with each epoch, you will enjoy compiling DSPy programs! I haven’t personally been as excited since training my first CIFAR-10 classifier with Keras!
It is such an exciting time to be learning about DSPy! I am super grateful to everyone on the DSPy team and members of the DSPy community both on Twitter/X and Discord, who have all helped tremendously in developing my understanding of the tool! We are just scratching the surface with DSPy and there is so much more to come! Here is the video, I hope you find it useful! 🎙️

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
RAG From Scratch: Indexing w/ ColBERT
Our RAG From Scratch video series walks through impt RAG concepts in short / focused videos w/ code.
This is the 14th video in our series and focuses on indexing with ColBERT for fine-grained similarity search.
🔧 Problem: Embedding models compress text into fixed-length (vector) representations that capture the semantic content of the document. This compression is very useful for efficient search / retrieval, but puts a heavy burden on that single vector representation to capture all the semantic nuance / detail of the doc. In some cases, irrelevant (to a query) / redundant content can dilute the semantic usefulness of the embedding for retrieval.
💡 Idea: ColBERT (@lateinteraction & @matei_zaharia) is a neat approach to address this with a higher granularity embedding approach: (1) produce a contextually influenced embedding for each token in the document and query. (2) score similarity between each query token and all document tokens. (3) take the max. (4) do this for all query tokens. (5) take the sum of the max scores (in step 3) for all query tokens to get a query-document similarity score. This granular token-wise similarity scoring between document and query has shown strong performance.

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
📢 Excited to finally be releasing my NeurIPS 2024 submission!
Is Chinchilla universal? No! We find that:
1. language model scaling laws depend on data complexity
2. gzip effectively predicts scaling properties from training data
As compressibility 📉, data preference 📈.
🧵⬇️
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GOpHYwBa8AA9HgG.jpg
Quoting @khoomeik
Say your training compute budget = ~1.5e13 FLOPs
If your dataset has a gzip compressibility ratio of 0.14, you should *max out your param count* and skimp on dataset size
But if your dataset is less compressible (gzip=0.61), *keep your model small* and train it on a ton of data
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GJEu4DUbEAAEXQS.png
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GJEu4DlawAAqC0F.png

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
Introducing The AI Scientist: The world’s first AI system for automating scientific research and open-ended discovery!
From ideation, writing code, running experiments and summarizing results, to writing entire papers and conducting peer-review, The AI Scientist opens a new era of AI-driven scientific research and accelerated discovery.
Here are 4 example Machine Learning research papers generated by The AI Scientist.
We published our report, The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery, and open-sourced our project!
Paper:
GitHub:
Our system leverages LLMs to propose and implement new research directions. Here, we first apply The AI Scientist to conduct Machine Learning research. Crucially, our system is capable of executing the entire ML research lifecycle: from inventing research ideas and experiments, writing code, to executing experiments on GPUs and gathering results. It can also write an entire scientific paper, explaining, visualizing and contextualizing the results.
Furthermore, while an LLM author writes entire research papers, another LLM reviewer critiques resulting manuscripts to provide feedback to improve the work, and also to select the most promising ideas to further develop in the next iteration cycle, leading to continual, open-ended discoveries, thus emulating the human scientific community. As a proof of concept, our system produced papers with novel contributions in ML research domains such language modeling, Diffusion and Grokking.
We (@_chris_lu_, @RobertTLange, @hardmaru) proudly collaborated with the @UniOfOxford (@j_foerst, @FLAIR_Ox) and @UBC (@cong_ml, @jeffclune) on this exciting project.

summary:
Nice to see that my soft-released optimizer library is proving useful.
Sometime in the near future I'll write a "release" blog post, but until then you can check out the docs here:
Quoting @dk21
Notes from LMSYS - Chatbot Arena Human Preference Predictions @kaggle competition top solutions (I didn’t participate). Goal is to predict which LLM response to a user prompt is better (as judged by Chat Arena users). Needs to be optimized to run for limited time on Kaggle (2xT4 GPUs). Tricks and findings:
- Distillation from larger models (70B > 9B) for the 1st place team
- Pseudo-labeling (similar to distillation except the signal is less granular) for many other top teams
- Averaging LORA weights across 5-fold trained models (!)
- With BF16 and optimizer with kahan summation support, it's possible to train 7B models using single A100 80G, 9B models requires two A100s. Found this great implementation by @benjamin_warner:
- Many top teams started fine-tuning from reward models (vs. instruct models)
- Adding to reading backlog - reward modeling approach, from the models used by many top teams:
- Adding to reading backlog - tascj training code
- Many teams disabled the softcapping on Gemma2 without hurt to performance
- Many teams struggled with finetuning Gemma2-27B
There was a bit of drama with a leak revealed last moment, but seems to have been resolved well. Congrats to the participants and winners!

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
Here is some ColPali news from today's exploration on DocVQA with @vespaengine, where we binarize the image patch embeddings (colpali 1.1) and evaluate pooling.
128 float nDCG@5 54.4
128 bit nDCG@5 52.4
Storage reduced by 32x. 270ms with a single CPU thread.
Then we evaluated the pooling technique from @bclavie
128 float nDCG@5 53.7
128 bit nDCG@5 51.5
With pooling, we reduce the number of patch vectors by 3x, and the latency drops by 3x and below 100ms (still single thread). This combination reduces storage by 96x (binarization + pooling) with only a 5% drop in nDCG@5 ranking accuracy. It might be worth it.

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
Here's why ColBERT embeddings are all the rage right now (at an intuitive level):
You probably already know that vector search is pretty cool.
• It allows you to search for things semantically.
• It's robust to synonyms.
But do you know what sucks about vector search?
It kind of lacks a certain degree of explainability.
The kind of explainability you'd, for example, have in keyword search:
There, you can see which keywords match between the query and the result.
ColBERT embeddings enable some explainability in vector search.
This is because
• Conventional dense embeddings: pool the token-level embeddings to a single representation.
• ColBERT embeddings: Keep the token-level embedding representation
We'll get to the technical details of ColBERT and the late interaction mechanism in another post, so stay tuned.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GWtj2l8WsAAAve7.png

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
I have received so many questions about document AI so answering here 📑💗
> I need structured input/output (e.g. invoices and JSON output of numbers from it) and I have labelled data, what do I do?
- Fine-tune following models and test, they have similar performance to each other: UDOP, Florence-2, LayoutLM3, PaliGemma
> I don't have labelled data OR I need to do document question answering on a document with charts, tables OR the task requires visual reasoning, math
- Try one of the big VLMs out of the box: Qwen2-VL, DocOwl, latest Llava, Idefics3 (best in math)
> I don't have labelled data but my input/outputs are structured
- you can label data with the models in answer 2 and then fine-tune models in answer 1. will dramatically cut costs
> I have a bunch of documents to do question answering from with no structured answer
- do multimodal RAG with ColPali and any VLM of your choice
needless to say do not give your important documents to proprietary models like gpt-4o (I will not answer any question that says why not use gpt-4o thx)

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
3 types of interaction in dense retrievers:
(or "what the heck is late interaction?!")
If you haven't been living under a rock, you've probably already heard of "late interaction".
It's the new mechanism introduced in the ColBERT paper.
But what exactly is late interaction?
"Interaction" describes to the process of assessing how well a document matches a given query by comparing their representations.
Here are 3 types of interaction in dense retrievers:
(a) No interaction:
- Process the query and documents separately.
- Fast similarity matching and computational efficiency
- But might miss contextual nuances and relationships between query and document
(b) All-to-all interaction:
- Process the query and documents together.
- Contextually rich
- But computationally expensive and difficult to scale
- Also called "early Interaction" or "full interaction"
- Examples: BERT, DPR
(c) Late interaction
- Interaction occurs after the query and document have been processed separately
- Contextually rich
- More computationally efficient and scalable than all-to-all interaction
- Examples: ColBERT
Now you know!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GX2HNXNWkAI0g-O.png

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
Ok, I’ll bite: What’s ColPali?
(And why should anyone working with RAG over PDFs care?)
ColPali makes information retrieval from complex document types - like PDFs - easier.
Information retrieval from PDFs is hard because they contain various components:
Text, images, tables, different headings, captions, complex layouts, etc.
For this, parsing PDFs currently requires multiple complex steps:
1. OCR
2. Layout recognition
3. Figure captioning
4. Chunking
5. Embedding
Not only are these steps complex and time-consuming, but they are also prone to error.
This is where ColPali comes into play.
But what is ColPali?
ColPali combines:
• Col -> the contextualized late interaction mechanism introduced in ColBERT
• Pali -> with a Vision Language Model (VLM), in this case, PaliGemma
And how does it work?
During indexing, the complex PDF parsing steps are replaced by using "screenshots" of the PDF pages directly.
These screenshots are then embedded with the VLM. At inference time, the query is embedded and matched with a late interaction mechanism to retrieve the most similar document pages.

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
This gradient accumulation implementation bug doesn't affect all training frameworks. For example, Composer has the accumulate_train_batch_on_tokens option, which should prevent this issue. I would be surprised if other training frameworks didn't have similar options.
Quoting @danielhanchen
Fixed a bug which caused all training losses to diverge for large gradient accumulation sizes.
1. First reported by @bnjmn_marie, GA is supposed to be mathematically equivalent to full batch training, but losses did not match.
2. We reproed the issue, and further investigation showed the L2 Norm betw bsz=16 and ga=16 was 10x larger.
3. The culprit was the cross entropy loss normalizer.
4. We ran training runs with denormalized CE Loss, and all training losses match.
5. We then re-normalized CE Loss with the correct denominator across all gradient accumulation steps, and verified all training loss curves match now.
6. We've already updated @UnslothAI with the fix, and wrote up more details in our blog post here:
This issue impacts all libraries which use GA, and simple averaging of GA does not work for varying sequence lengths.
This also impacts DDP and multi GPU training which accumulates gradients. Please update Unsloth via pip install --upgrade --no-cache-dir unsloth and use from unsloth import unsloth_train
We have a Colab notebook using our fixed GA: and a Kaggle notebook:

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
What is the “Col” in ColBERT and ColPali? ⬇️
Contextualized Late Interaction (Col) is used in models like ColBERT for text retrieval and ColPali for vision-based tasks, and it combines the high performance of cross-encoder models with the computational efficiency of bi-encoders.
Instead of performing an all-to-all comparison of query and document tokens at runtime like BERT-based systems, Col pre-computes and stores document token embeddings offline, while still having high accuracy like cross encoders!
The MaxSim (Maximum Similarity) operation is the secret sauce of “Col” methods - for each query token, MaxSim calculates its similarity with every token in a document using dot product, then selects the highest score. The final similarity score between the query and document is the sum of these MaxSim scores for all query tokens.

title: @bclavie
summary: 🐭byaldi v0.0.7 is out! It's been a while, so time for a re-introduction: 🐭byaldi is a library that makes it ridiculously easy to use models with complex mechanisms, so you don't have to understand what a "late-interaction multi-modal VLM-based retrievers" * is before you can try out what they allow you to do. ❓And what do they allow you to do? It's simple: thanks to such models, you can search through your entire messy document collection composed of graphs, image PDFs that were scanned in 1978, powerpoint slide decks with a font that OCR systems have officially surrendered to, and many more previously-hated document formats. 📄It does so with no pre-processing: you just need to pass the document, as an image, to the model, to be encoded and indexed. Afterwards, you can query your collection with natural text, and get the relevant pages back, ready to be fed onto one of the many vision-equipped LLMs now around (GPT4o, Claude Sonnet 3.5, Llama 3.2, Qwen2-VL, etc...) 🎣 So what's the catch? There's none, except that multi-modal retrieval is brand new, so it's experiencing some growing pains, as you would expect: sometimes the model isn't actually great at adapting to your domain, and handling large indexes is still tough, but we are making quick progress on these! If you can't wait to jump in, just head to our github and check out our example notebook or @mervenoyann's intro to open-source multi-modal RAG to see how easy it is to get started. 🔗 Example notebook: @mervenoyann's introductory notebook: Main repo: * of course, I think all of those are really cool. @lateinteraction is a very important mechanism to understand documents at a fine-grained level, and multi-modal retrievers and LLMs are the future, as per @mervenoyann

linked_urls.title: Beyond the Basics of RAG – Parlance
linked_urls.summary: LLMs are powerful, but have limitations: their knowledge is fixed in their weights, and their context window is limited. Worse: when they don’t know something, they might just make it up. RAG, for Retrieval Augmented Generation, has emerged as a way to mitigate both of those problems. However, implementing RAG effectively is more complex than it seems. The nitty gritty parts of what makes good retrieval good are rarely talked about: No, cosine similarity is, in fact, not all you need. In this workshop, we explore what helps build a robust RAG pipeline, and how simple insights from retrieval research can greatly improve your RAG efforts. We’ll cover key topics like BM25, re-ranking, indexing, domain specificity, evaluation beyond LGTM@few, and filtering. Be prepared for a whole new crowd of incredibly useful buzzwords to enter your vocabulary.

At this point we have a large and loyal paid community, we build tons of features for them (I think we did >30 releases this year) and they're pretty happy. We have enough revenue to fund tons of crazy R&D and our models are still the best by the metrics we care about (how the images look and how fun it is to make things). We have a huge backlog of exciting things to make our models way better. Zero risk. We did all this with no investors. Honestly, it feels like we are successful. The next metric of success I think about most about is now that we have "all I ever wanted" in terms of a big well funded R&D lab with cool people free to work on whatever we want... title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
After six years, we FINALLY have a worthy successor to BERT
Here's why modernBERT is revolutionizing encoder models 🔽
What was improved?
- 𝗔𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲: Now using Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) for better positional understanding, and a streamlined architecture with fewer bias terms.
- 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲: handles up to 8,192 tokens (16x larger than traditional encoders), runs up to 4x faster for mixed-length inputs (compared to DeBERTa), and uses less memory while achieving better performance.
- 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗙𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀: Alternating attention patterns, efficient sequence packing and unpadding (reduces computational waste), optimized for common inference GPUs
- 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀: Trained on 2 trillion tokens from diverse sources including code, scientific articles, and web documents, with a 30% masking rate and three-phase training process with long-context adaptation.
⭐ Particularly shines with:
- RAG pipelines requiring longer context
- code search and understanding
- enterprise-scale retrieval systems
- classification tasks needing both speed and accuracy
The best part is you can use it as a drop-in replacement for BERT-like models in both base (149M params) and large (395M params) variants.

title: @bclavie
summary: 🧵 Stella Embeddings: What's the big deal? (a mini explanation thread) If you enjoy RAG Twitter, or compulsively check the MTEB leaderboard, you might've come across the "Stella" (and now, Jasper) models. They seem suspiciously good, even though you've never heard of them before. Well, let's begin with a spoiler: they're good, period. ✨ Stella is really cool, for a few reasons: - It's a piece of independent research into topics that aren't the current mainstream way of doing things, with fantastic results to back it up - It's specifically designed to avoid overfitting and maximize generalization 🏆 Let's take a step back to understand a big piece of signal that makes the Stella embeddings special: MTEB MTEB is the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark. It's a set of curated datasets designed to evaluate embedding models' capabilities on various tasks, including a mix of retrieval tasks. It's essentially the go-to when you're trying to figure out what embedding model you should try. 🤔 If you occasionally glance at the IR people Twitter discussions, you'll see that MTEB is a pretty disputed hot topic. That's because there are a lot of different setups co-existing on a single leaderboard: - Some models attempt to be truly zero-shot (MTEB was designed as a zero-shot eval, but has a sizeable trainset) - Some models train on some subsets/all of it, in various ways. ⚠️ Don't get me wrong: training on the training set is good, actually. It's valuable signal towards the potential of a model when finetuned on domain-appropriate data. There's absolutely nothing wrong with overfitting MTEB, in a vacuum. The problem is that they're all blended together on the same leaderboard: it's impossible to tell who's doing what, and what level of contamination you should expect for each model. Is this model lagging behind because it's worse? Or because it's fully zero-shot? Nobody knows. 🔍 Now then, let's look at how embedding models are usually trained: The current dominant way of training retrieval models is via the use of a contrastive loss, with little-to-no knowledge distillation (except some, such as ColBERT and ColBERTv2, or RocketQA, but it's very rarely used by MTEB mainstays). The contrastive process uses Query <-> Document relationships, with a two-step approach: 1️⃣ First, use a lot of distantly supervised data to align the model's embedding space onto the concept of "similarity" between documents and queries. This'll be stuff like a Reddit title and its comments, Title <-> Abstract pairs from SemanticScholars, etc. 2️⃣ Then, fine-tune on higher quality annotated data, either extracted from a search engine based on which documents users clicked on after their search. Or, more generally, any dataset where human annotators labeled that the document is an answer to the query. 💭 In my opinion (and I backed it up with answerai-colbert-small!) distillation should have a bigger place. This is especially true nowadays that we have LLM-based embedders, which can be very good, but also very, very impractical given their size. ✨ And you know what? This is where Stella enters the arena! Stella's approach takes distillation even further than previous methods: what if we only use unsupervised distillation? Why don't we get rid of those expensive, pesky labels, and complicated hard negative mining pipelines? (spoilers: this is a good idea): 🔮 Essentially, Stella takes a few really good 7B LLM-based embedding models and comes up with a multi-step learning process, involving freezing/unfreezing, dimension manipulation tricks, and much more: read the paper to find out! 📐 The main aim of this training is to work within the embedding space, seeking to minimize the geometric distances (both cosine and angular distance) between the teachers' vectors and the student model (Stella)'s outputs. 🤖 The resulting model is one that has never itself been trained on predicting query <-> document relationships like a normal retrieval model would, but instead has learned to mimic how models much smarter than itself would represent both queries and documents. 🎯 In practice, Stella models generalize amazingly well because of this. Most other small models overfit on MTEB in some ways, consciously or not: either by training on its data or, in the case of some models, by iterating on the synthetic data mix they use and selecting the one that has the best MTEB dev score. This generally makes it kinda hard to know what's the best model for downstream use: is the model really good at generalization (what 99% of people want for their own use cases) or is the model really well fitted to MTEB? (As discussed above, this is useful signal in itself, but a lot of people want to use off-the-shelf embeddings and that's it, in which case, this is not an appropriate signal) 💫 Stella doesn't really have that problem: it's good at MTEB because it's good at generating representations that look like its teacher models' representations, and its teacher models' representations are good because they are gigantic models that are at least 7x, oftentimes 20-30x, bigger than common retrieval models. Stella isn't trained on MTEB; at worst, it's picked up some of what its teachers knew about it. But thankfully, the teachers selected weren't overfitted on MTEB. 🎉 This means that the signal you get from Stella doing well on MTEB is that much more meaningful: you know for a fact it's good at generalizing, and so intuitively, it's a good starting point for your task. (This has been anecdotally verified quite a few times -- on the new TREC RAG datasets, and I've heard from a bunch of people in various industries who got great results by just swapping in the latest Stella model instead of whatever they were using before)

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
Some quick thoughts: On why we gave the ColBERT paradigm the name "late interaction" instead of "multi-vector", a term that emerged later and that has proven to be more intuitive.
**The mechains is actually not about having multiple vectors at all.** You can see this in four different ways.
1) You can take a ColBERT-like method and try to use a constant number of vectors (e.g., 16) but it will barely outperform having one vector in the general case.
It's not that you need token-level alignment per se (you don't either!) but you want fine-grained representations, not just *multiple* representations.
2) More importantly, there's nothing to say you can't store a TON of information in a single vector. Similarly, it's easy to use multiple vectors and gain *zero* improvement over a single-vector, e.g. if you replace MaxSim with AvgSim in ColBERT, without any other changes, it doesn't work!
The problem isn't the vector representation, it's the **learnability of the scoring function**.
A dot product is just very hard to learn. An intuition I learned from Menon et al (2021) is that: for dot products, every time you "fix" one query--document pair, you likely break so many other pairs by moving the query and/or document representations.
For ColBERT, you typically *fix* more than you break because you're moving *tokens* in a much smaller (and far more composable!) space.
3) "Multi-vector" makes it sound like these approaches win because they store "more stuff".
But that's actually not true: if you look at how aggressively compressed typical ColBERT implementations (like PLAID) are, it's often as small as 20 bytes per vector (that's like 5 floats), which makes a document representation often far smaller than the uncompressed single-vector variants people usually deploy.
4) By default, IR methods that use "multiple vectors" (e.g., cross-encoders) are unscalable. The fascinating thing in late interaction is that it's easy to implement in asymptotically sub-linear ways thank to pruning. THAT is worth a lot.
Anyway, it's no big deal, but the term late interaction > multi-vector, in principle, though multi-vector is a lot more intuitive and sticks.
Quoting @lateinteraction
A lesson reconfirmed dozens of times in IR: granular scoring generalizes far better than dense dot products when tasks are hard. Late interaction ftw!

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
A solution for better search results:
Late interaction preserves contextual nuances that pooling (as in most dense vector retrieval models) destroys. How?
There are three different ways retrieval models handle the "interaction" between your query and potential documents:
1️⃣ 𝗡𝗼-𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀: Traditional dense vector search where both query and documents are pooled into single vectors. Fast but loses contextual nuance.
2️⃣ 𝗙𝘂𝗹𝗹-𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀: Process query and document together with cross-attention. Contextually rich but computationally expensive at query time.
3️⃣ 𝗟𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀: The best of both worlds. They precompute token-level embeddings for documents but delay the interaction to query time.
Instead of pooling token embeddings into a single vector, late interaction models keep representations for each token and use a MaxSim operator to find the best matches between query and document tokens. This preserves contextual relationships while remaining computationally efficient.
There’s three main late interaction models:
𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗕𝗘𝗥𝗧 (Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT):
- Text-only model fine-tuned from BERT
- Stores token-level embeddings (vs single document vectors)
𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗣𝗮𝗹𝗶 (Contextualized Late Interaction over PaliGemma):
- Multimodal model using PaliGemma as its foundation
- Processes documents as images, dividing them into patches
- Can handle complex pdfs with text, tables, and graphics without separate OCR
- ~3B parameters with 128-dimension embeddings
𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗤𝘄𝗲𝗻 (Contextualized Late Interaction over Qwen2):
- Similar to ColPali but uses Qwen2 Vision LLM instead
- Slightly smaller at ~2B parameters
- Licensed under permissive Apache 2.0
The storage cost is the main trade-off with these models. Since they store embeddings for each token/patch rather than a single vector per document, they require more memory. However, techniques like quantization and residual compression can reduce this footprint by a lot
Read more in this blog:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GoGX80QWMAAjIYP.png

LLMを用いた高度な金融タスクを解決することを目指して、EDINET-Benchを開発・公開しました！
研究開発に無料で利用できる金融データセットが少ない中、金融庁が公開しているEDINETをフル活用した自動ラベリングにより、複数タスクのデータセットを自動作成できるようにしています！
Quoting @SakanaAILabs
日本語金融ベンチマーク「EDINET-Bench」を公開
ブログ：
論文：
金融庁の電子開示システムであるEDINETの有価証券報告書を活用し、高度な金融タスクにてAIがどの程度対応できるかを測るための日本語金融ベンチマークを構築しました。
EDINET-Bench での評価の結果、現状のLLMを単純に適用するだけでは、会計不正検知等において実用的な性能は出ないという課題が確認された一方、入力情報を工夫することによる性能向上の可能性も示唆されました。今後、本ベンチマーク、およびそこで得た知見を活かし、金融タスクによりよく対応できる特化型LLMの開発を進めていきます。
論文・データセット・コードも公開しています。本研究が日本の金融業界におけるLLM活用の加速の一助となれば幸いです。Sakana AIは引き続き、金融をはじめとする日本の各産業におけるAI活用を加速させるための研究開発を進めてまいります。
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gs9xfmybIAEBYzI.jpg

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
For those confused about all the AI terms, it's all just "search"
RAG -> semantic search across embeddings
State/history -> cached searches that die after the task
Memory -> searching user "policies" or "rules", typically keyword and join-based
Prompt -> latent search over the probability space of the LLM model
Structured Outputs -> search completions (it's literally autocompleting an output from the given search queries)
And the rest is just normal software engineering

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] Retweet @HamelHusain
In our rage against "RAG is Dead", @bclavie and I assembled annotated talk notes (Simon Williston style). We take you through the many reasons why RAG is just getting started: single dense vector representations are quite naive
Notes in reply
────────
[2/2] Retweet @HamelHusain
Overview of the series
1. We’ve been measuring wrong. @beirmug showed that traditional IR metrics optimize for finding the #1 result. RAG needs different goals: coverage (getting all the facts), diversity (corroborating facts), and relevance. Models that ace BEIR benchmarks often fail at real RAG tasks.
2. Retrieval can reason. @orionweller 's models understand instructions like “find documents about data privacy using metaphors.” His Rank1 system generates explicit reasoning traces about relevance. These models find documents that traditional systems never surface.
3. Single vectors lose information. @antoine_chaffin demonstrated how late-interaction models like ColBERT preserve token-level information. No more forcing everything into one conflicted representation. Result: 150M parameter models outperforming 7B parameter alternatives on reasoning tasks.
4. One map isn’t enough. @BEBischof and @loldedxd showed why we need multiple representations. Their art search demo finds the same painting through literal descriptions, poetic interpretations, or similar images—each using different indices. Stop searching for the perfect embedding. Build specialized representations and route intelligently.
Annotated slides can be found here:

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
I especially enjoyed the conversation with Antoine on "why aren't late interaction models more popular"**
(**they're downloaded >20M times per month, but one may ask why isn't it 200M!)
Rant that may be useful for others thinking about different problems:
My take on that is that most people satisfice. Think of someone who's just learned about RAG (and thinks it means dense retrievers) and is now are trying to use them to solve *their* problem.
If out of the blue you're telling them about this whole other retrieval paradigm, whoa, cognitive overload. Now you're saying they need to use a different library for it to work? Nah, they don't want the quality gain badly enough for this software risk.
Notions like storage and latency aren't really relevant to long-tail adoption here IMO.
Even a basic PLAID index from 2022 is *far* faster and more space-efficient than the *average* dense retrieval system deployed with NumPy-like basic representations! Back in 2022, we used a single CPU-only server to search >100 MILLION pages with PLAID in like 200 milliseconds. Without a GPU. (With something like our latest WARP, it's another 3x faster.)
It's just a different paradigm, and adoption of new ML paradigms that involve a new software stack is rarely about the merits. It takes community building, software building, and repeated results-backed hype until enough copy-paste pipelines trickle down to the masses... to really mainstream stuff!
But by that level of mainstream-ing, adoption stops being connected to the merits, so all the fun and community is gone by then, if you ask me.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GvxpzbnW8AAy_iu.png

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
This is not a major problem among us ML twitter nerds, but it's awful in enterprise settings.
Very common situation: Boss comes in, tells engs they should use the new Llama/Qwen/etc they read about on LinkedIn, it works 30% better than [whatever we were using]!
The reality: They're still using a finetuned Mistral 7B or Llama3 because there's no time on the engineering roadmap dedicated to "figuring out how to fine-tune an MoE" or "I really don't understand why Gemma is not fine-tuning properly these params used to work I swear".
Especially when historically, "just take our data and feed it to a better model" has been the norm. It's a nightmare for engineers to explain that this just doesn't work these days, because trying to use a model from a different family (or even generation, you can't FT qwen3 exactly the same way you FT'd qwen2) comes with a whole new set of issues.
Quoting @bclavie
Not to sound like a DSPy shill, but a gigantic pro of stuff like MIPRO/GEPA (cc @LakshyAAAgrawal @lateinteraction) is that it doesn't come with major suffering if you ever want to use use newer/better models.
FT/RL is fun, but upgrading your model family is exceedingly painful.

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
For over a year, @jeremyphoward has been in stealth mode. In this exclusive talk, he showcases what he's been working on.
He & @johnowhitaker show us SolveIt, a new dev environment and programming paradigm.
🤯 Imagine this workflow:
- Build a web app & interact with its UI on the same screen as your code. No more flipping to a separate browser.
- Use live variables from your REPL directly in prompts to the AI. The AI knows your current state.
- Turn any Python function into an AI tool instantly. No no registering tools or MCP. Just write a function in a cell and tell the AI to use it.
This is a live, malleable environment that fuses the best ideas from Literate Programming (Knuth), the live-object world of Smalltalk, and the interactive cells of Jupyter.
Who is Solveit for?
Jeremy's take: SolveIt is best for programmers who are either very new (< 3 years) or very experienced (> 20 years). Why? Because developers in the middle (3-20 years) often have ingrained workflows and can find this different paradigm confronting. New devs are open-minded and build good habits from scratch, while veterans immediately recognize how this approach solves decades-old problems of complexity and state management.
My Thoughts
It's early days, but it is super cool. You get all the fun of trying a new programming language without learning new syntax (Python), because it will show you new patterns and ways of doing this. If you are wiling to climb the learning curve it is an extremely powerful tool that you can be productive with on real tasks like writing and coding. I'm personally addicted to it for several workflows and am afraid of losing it tbh.
How Can You Try It?
Just follow @jeremyphoward - he will announce something in the coming weeks or months (I suspect if this post is popular he might do something soon 🤣 )

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
Lately I’ve been liking the idea of putting work out as blog post/arxivs/journal articles and kind of just attending conferences for the social aspect.
I feel like I haven’t gotten any value from confs on a scientific level in a few years: the best work is on arxiv and can be peer reviewed in journals for posterity’s sake, giving the reviewers time to truly engage with the work.
Conferences are increasingly feeling like the worst of every world to me: bad reviews because of the immense volumes, yet still too slow to be anywhere near as relevant as arxiv. I really felt this at ICLR: even many of the authors I spoke to barely cared about their poster anymore, the work was submitted 9 months ago, essentially a lifetime in this field.
OTOH I still feel like attending once or twice a year has immense collaborative value. I just increasingly feel like there’s a big masquerade around conference pubs due to inertia, when realistically being accepted at a conference doesn’t really mean anything regarding a paper’s quality anymore.

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
Your periodic reminder that late interaction isn’t “awesome but takes a lot of space” as I see here often.
ColBERT vectors are often 10 bytes each. Ten bytes. That’s like 3-4 floats.
It’s about *interactions* (aka ~attention) not “many vectors”.
It’s not “many vectors work better than one vector”. It’s “set similarity works better and trains better than a rigid dot product”.
Even with the same storage cost! You can’t fix this by making one vector bigger. You don’t need a lot of storage of the mini-vectors for late interaction.
It’s just that dot products suck.

What if scaling the context windows of frontier LLMs is much easier than it sounds?
We’re excited to share our work on Recursive Language Models (RLMs). A new inference strategy where LLMs can decompose and recursively interact with input prompts of seemingly unbounded length, as a REPL environment.
On the OOLONG benchmark, RLMs with GPT-5-mini outperforms GPT-5 by over 110% gains (more than double!) on 132k-token sequences and is cheaper to query on average.
On the BrowseComp-Plus benchmark, RLMs with GPT-5 can take in 10M+ tokens as their “prompt” and answer highly compositional queries without degradation and even better than explicit indexing/retrieval.

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
What I think about retrieval for LLMs/agents🤔:
Since LLMs can scan all top-k documents in the search result, information overlap is strictly useless.
Instead, what is important for LLMs is to not miss important information. Missing one key fact can flip a decision, even if everything else was “relevant.”
For example, you ask an agent, “Should death penalty be allowed?” The agent searches and gives an opinion.
But the agent misses critical information while searching: "The death penalty is about 2-3× more expensive than life imprisonment." (which is true, apparently)
This information about cost is critical for this debate, but the agent must decide without considering this missing information.
Q: Then, what should we do?
A: We should build retrievers that minimize missing relevant information, instead of naively maximizing relevance.
I think there should be an independent benchmark for this path...
That was my initial thought before writing this paper, but for clarity, I decided not to relate it to LLMs😅. And this is because I identified a critical flaw in the existing diversity design.
So, I wrote about LLMs-link here instead.
Quoting @rikiyatakehi
Our full paper was accepted to WSDM 2026 🎉
We identify crucial vulnerabilities in existing diversification and propose to minimize the risk of overlooking query intents.
Minimizing this risk matters also when LLMs/agents perform retrieval, because they can read all top-k documents, where information overlap brings little value.
Preprint at the end! 🧵

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
(1/n) 🚨 BERTs that chat: turn any BERT into a chatbot with diffusion
hi @karpathy, we just trained a few BERTs to chat with diffusion — we are releasing all the model checkpoints, training curves, and recipes! Hopefully this spares you the side quest into training nanochat with diffusion for now 🙂. It’s both a hands-on tutorial for beginners and an example showing how to use our complete toolkit (dLLM) for deeper projects.
Code:
Report:
Checkpoints:
Motivation: I couldn’t find a good “Hello World” example for training a minimally working yet useful diffusion language models, a class of bidirectional language models capable of parallel token generation in arbitrary order. So I tried finetuning BERTs to make it chat with discrete diffusion—and it turned out more fun than I expected.
TLDR: With a small amount of open-source instruction-following data, a standard BERT can gain conversational ability with diffusion. Specifically, a finetuned ModernBERT-large, with a similar number of parameters, performs close to Qwen1.5-0.5B.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/1988287081538596864/img/Bymco1gbvg91ZiCU.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/1988287081538596864/vid/avc1/320x324/Wvf4b9J6vVAt2UVT.mp4?tag=21
Quoting @karpathy
Nice, short post illustrating how simple text (discrete) diffusion can be.
Diffusion (i.e. parallel, iterated denoising, top) is the pervasive generative paradigm in image/video, but autoregression (i.e. go left to right bottom) is the dominant paradigm in text. For audio I've seen a bit of both.
A lot of diffusion papers look a bit dense but if you strip the mathematical formalism, you end up with simple baseline algorithms, e.g. something a lot closer to flow matching in continuous, or something like this in discrete. It's your vanilla transformer but with bi-directional attention, where you iteratively re-sample and re-mask all tokens in your "tokens canvas" based on a noise schedule until you get the final sample at the last step. (Bi-directional attention is a lot more powerful, and you get a lot stronger autoregressive language models if you train with it, unfortunately it makes training a lot more expensive because now you can't parallelize across sequence dim).
So autoregression is doing an `.append(token)` to the tokens canvas while only attending backwards, while diffusion is refreshing the entire token canvas with a `.setitem(idx, token)` while attending bidirectionally. Human thought naively feels a bit more like autoregression but it's hard to say that there aren't more diffusion-like components in some latent space of thought. It feels quite possible that you can further interpolate between them, or generalize them further. And it's a component of the LLM stack that still feels a bit fungible.
Now I must resist the urge to side quest into training nanochat with diffusion.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/G3uRtoLWgAMaMa6.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/tweet_video/G3uRtoLWgAMaMa6.mp4

summary:
[1/2] Retweet @peter_richtarik
I am an AC for ICLR 2026. One of the papers in my batch was just withdrawn. The authors wrote a brief response, explaining why the reviewers failed at their job. I agree with most of their comments. The authors gave up. They are fed up. Just like many of us. I understand. We pretend the emperor has clothes, but he is naked.
Here is the final part of their withdrawal notice. I took the liberty to make it public, to highlight that what we are doing with AI conference reviews these last few years is, basically, madness.
---
Comment: We thank the reviewers for their time.
However, upon reading the reviews for our paper, it became immediately apparent that the four "reject" ratings are not based on good-faith academic disagreement, but on a critical failure to read the submitted paper.
The reviews are rife with demonstrably false claims that are directly contradicted by the text. The core justifications for rejection rely on asserting that key components are "missing" when they are explicitly detailed in the manuscript. Some specific examples are (and many are even fake claims).
Claim: Harder tasks like GSM8K are missing.
Fact: GSM8K results are in many tables, like Table 2 (Section 4.2) and Appendix G.
Claim: The method does not use per-layer ranks.
Fact: This is the entire point of our method. The reviewer clearly mistook our method for the baselines. (Section 2, Table 1).
Claim: The GP kernel is not specified.
Fact: It is specified in Appendix E (Table 6).
Claim: There is no ablation of the method's three stages.
Fact: Section 4.4 ("Ablation Study") and Appendix J are dedicated to this.
Reviewers have a fundamental responsibility to read and evaluate the work they are assigned. The nature of these errors is so fundamental, so systemic in overlooking explicit content, that it goes far beyond what "limited time" or "oversight" can explain. This work has gone through several rounds of revision over the last year. In earlier submissions, the paper usually received borderline or weak-accept scores.
Numerous signs strongly suggest that some reviewers are relying entirely on AI tools to automatically generate peer reviews, rather than fulfilling their fundamental responsibility of personally reading and evaluating manuscripts.
We strongly protest this.
This is a gross disrespect to the authors. It is a flagrant desecration of the reviewer's sacred duty. It fundamentally undermines the integrity of the entire peer-review process.
Given that the reviews are not based on the actual content of our paper, we have decided to withdraw the submission.
We leave this comment so that future readers of the OpenReview page are aware that the items described as "missing" are already present in the submitted manuscript. These negative reviews for this submission are factually unsound and do not reflect the content of the paper. We cannot and will not accept an assessment that is not based on the work we actually submitted.
────────
[2/2] Retweet @peter_richtarik

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
I spent a long time thinking about this post. I genuinely do not understand how one can hold this view, even as a purposefully exaggerated argument.
Curing cancer, etc, has lives on the line. Every single day it’s not cured, thousands suffer and die.
There’s no “joy of research” worth this price. If any researcher is offered the choice between curing cancer and keeping their job, it would be an immense act of cruelty to even hesitate.
Quoting @togelius
I was at an event on AI for science yesterday, a panel discussion here at NeurIPS. The panelists discussed how they plan to replace humans at all levels in the scientific process. So I stood up and protested that what they are doing is evil. Look around you, I said. The room is filled with researchers of various kinds, most of them young. They are here because they love research and want to contribute to advancing human knowledge. If you take the human out of the loop, meaning that humans no longer have any role in scientific research, you're depriving them of the activity they love and a key source of meaning in their lives. And we all want to do something meaningful. Why, I asked, do you want to take the opportunity to contribute to science away from us?
My question changed the course of the panel, and set the tone for the rest of the discussion. Afterwards, a number of attendees came up to me, either to thank me for putting what they felt into words, or to ask if I really meant what I said. So I thought I would return to the question here.
One of the panelists asked whether I would really prefer the joy of doing science to finding a cure for cancer and enabling immortality. I answered that we will eventually cure cancer and at some point probably be able to choose immortality. Science is already making great progress with humans at the helm. We'll get fusion power and space travel some day as well. Maybe cutting humans out of the loop could speed up this process, but I don't think it would be worth it. I think it is of crucial importance that we humans are in charge of our own progress. Expanding humanity's collective knowledge is, I think, the most meaningful thing we can do. If humans could not usefully contribute to science anymore, this would be a disaster. So, no. I do not think it worth it to find a cure for cancer faster if that means we can never do science again.
Many of those who came up to talk to me last night, those who asked me whether I was being serious or just trolling, thought that the premise was absurd. Of course there would always be room for humans in science. There will always be tasks only humans can do, insight only humans have, and so on. Therefore, we should welcome AI. Research is hard, and we need all the help we can get. I responded that I hoped they were right. That is, I truly hope there will always be parts of the research process which humans will be essential for. But what I was arguing against was not what we might call "weak science automation", where humans stay in the loop in important roles, but "strong science automation", where humans are redundant.
Others thought it was immature to argue about this, because full science automation is not on the horizon. Again, I hope they are right. But I see no harm in discussing it now. And I certainly don't think we need research on science automation to go any further.
Yet others remarked that this was a pointless argument. Science automation is coming whether we want it or not, and we'd better get used to it. The train is coming, and we can get on it or stand in its way. I think that is a remarkably cowardly argument. It is up to us as a society to decide how we use the technology we develop. It's not a train, it's a truck, and we'd better grab the steering wheel.
One of the panelists made a chess analogy, arguing that lots of people play chess even though computers are now much better than humans at chess. So we might engage in science as a kind of hobby, even though the real science is done by computers. We would be playing around far from the frontier, perhaps filling in the blanks that AI systems don't care about. That was, to put it mildly, not a satisfying answer. While I love games, I certainly do not consider game-playing as meaningful as advancing human knowledge. Thanks, but no thanks.
Overall, though, it was striking that most of those I talked to thanked me for raising the point, as I articulated worries that they already had. One of them remarked that if you work on automating science and are not even a little bit worried about the end goal, you are a psychopath. I would add that another possibility is that you don't really believe in what you are doing.
Some might ask why I make this argument about science and not, for example, about visual art, music, or game design. That's because yesterday's event was about AI for science. But I think the same argument applies to all domains of human creative and intellectual expression. Making human intellectual or creative work redundant is something we should avoid when we can, and we should absolutely avoid it if there are no equally meaningful new roles for humans to transition into.
You could further argue that working on cutting humans out of meaningful creative work such as scientific research is incredibly egoistic. You get the intellectual satisfaction of inventing new AI methods, but the next generation don't get a chance to contribute. Why do you want to rob your children (academic and biological) of the chance to engage in the most meaningful activity in the world?
So what do I believe in, given that I am an AI researcher who actively works on the kind of AI methods used for automating science? I believe that AI tools that help us be more productive and creative are great, but that AI tools that replace us are bad. I love science, and I am afraid of a future where we are pushed back into the dark ages because we can no longer contribute to science. Human agency, including in creative processes, is vital and must be safeguarded at almost any cost.
I don't exactly know how to steer AI development and AI usage so that we get new tools but are not replaced. But I know that it is of paramount importance.

Others thought it was immature to argue about this, because full science automation is not on the horizon. Again, I hope they are right. But I see no harm in discussing it now. And I certainly don't think we need research on science automation to go any further.
Yet others remarked that this was a pointless argument. Science automation is coming whether we want it or not, and we'd better get used to it. The train is coming, and we can get on it or stand in its way. I think that is a remarkably cowardly argument. It is up to us as a society to decide how we use the technology we develop. It's not a train, it's a truck, and we'd better grab the steering wheel.
One of the panelists made a chess analogy, arguing that lots of people play chess even though computers are now much better than humans at chess. So we might engage in science as a kind of hobby, even though the real science is done by computers. We would be playing around far from the frontier, perhaps filling in the blanks that AI systems don't care about. That was, to put it mildly, not a satisfying answer. While I love games, I certainly do not consider game-playing as meaningful as advancing human knowledge. Thanks, but no thanks.
Overall, though, it was striking that most of those I talked to thanked me for raising the point, as I articulated worries that they already had. One of them remarked that if you work on automating science and are not even a little bit worried about the end goal, you are a psychopath. I would add that another possibility is that you don't really believe in what you are doing.
Some might ask why I make this argument about science and not, for example, about visual art, music, or game design. That's because yesterday's event was about AI for science. But I think the same argument applies to all domains of human creative and intellectual expression. Making human intellectual or creative work redundant is something we should avoid when we can, and we should absolutely avoid it if there are no equally meaningful new roles for humans to transition into.
You could further argue that working on cutting humans out of meaningful creative work such as scientific research is incredibly egoistic. You get the intellectual satisfaction of inventing new AI methods, but the next generation don't get a chance to contribute. Why do you want to rob your children (academic and biological) of the chance to engage in the most meaningful activity in the world?
So what do I believe in, given that I am an AI researcher who actively works on the kind of AI methods used for automating science? I believe that AI tools that help us be more productive and creative are great, but that AI tools that replace us are bad. I love science, and I am afraid of a future where we are pushed back into the dark ages because we can no longer contribute to science. Human agency, including in creative processes, is vital and must be safeguarded at almost any cost.
I don't exactly know how to steer AI development and AI usage so that we get new tools but are not replaced. But I know that it is of paramount importance.

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
I did not quite read it as the core belief, but I can kind of understand why it could be.
In terms of the two core questions:
- I do not believe that we are likely to be pushed back to the dark ages, but I see your point about this being a disagreement about probabilities in this case. Evidently, Julian believes the probability is much higher than I do.
- More importantly, I do not currently have a strongly held prediction on whether or not we will ever be fully automated out of the scientific process. We will likely be automated away to some extent, but throughout times an increase of automation has most often resulted in new fields of study, new ways of doing things, etc... There's a case to be made that maybe this won't be the case with AI, and we will truly have automated scientific progress that abstracts humans away.
I do understand how one could be worried about this status quo being the dark ages, but it requires a few logical hoops to be jumped through to reach the conclusion that "Scientific progress is automated -> We reach new heights such as curing cancer (part of the thesis here) -> This comes at the cost of us no longer in charge -> This world in which curing cancer was fully automated somehow collapses into the dark ages."
It's definitely a possibility, I can't say for sure the probability is 0. I do think that deciding that the upsides (countless lives saved, with a probability of 100% if we accept the AIs can automated curing cancer, among other scientific progress) are not worth the downsides (loss of research joy and an unspecified, arguable potential collapse to the dark age) is a point of view I cannot morally support, and I feel like the point could've been made about any significant progress in mankind' history.
Countless inventions *could* theoretically have led to the dark ages. Famously, many researchers were suppressed on this fear. In the middle ages, studies of anatomy and the human bodies are widely opposed out of fear they would destroy an innate order and violate the reverence we had for life, stealing something essential. The printing press and the enlightenment were both opposed for threatening the order and the way of life. We had epidemics of "telegraph shock" and "railway madness" when electricity was spreading. Doctors and researchers in Pasteur's era vehemently opposed his work, especially on germ theory and standardisation of research, partly out of fears for how it would upset the existing methods.
The very thought that "this new development which will change the way things are done" will threaten the very fabric of society, and therefore we should hold back on it and not accept its obvious social benefits out of a potential fear, is essentially a timeless argument about new science. Interestingly, it's often made by those who did use to do good science, but dislike the implications of the new science on their own work, which does feel like a very human reaction.
I do like the old ways, to be honest. I'm anxious about certain aspects of the future. I still think it's an abhorrent and archaic view that we should not meaningfully improve the existence of people today out of a fear that, perhaps, things will be made worse, in some way. This argument is nothing new, it was made even in Plato's time, and one thing I do respect about Julian's post is that there is an aspect of candor in it: the argument is less thinly veiled than usual, as it does essentialy state that "the joy of research (my job) is worth the suffering of others", before landing on the usual "but imagine, maybe, there could be the dark ages! just like we had the dark ages with Galileo and Newton!".

Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
This is a single model study pushed out by UK govt official bodies, using small single-GPU models, with an extremely strongly worded conclusion that concludes that LLMs fail at crucially important real-world task.
I'm finding it increasingly worrying that so many studies of "LLMs applicability to [real important problem]" are done with government support (amazing) but without any apparent understanding of LLM ecosystems or best practices. Yet, they have a veneer of respectability due to institutional affiliations and will very likely be used to inform policy.
Just in this paper alone, beyond using weak models in the first place, there's a high reliance on very outdated prompting methods, giving a long list of instructions before begging the model to please output properly formatted json.
It also uses gpt-oss-120b itself to be the LLM judge in a highly specialised domain, though they do verify correlation w/ human judgements to an extent.
And yet, despite flaws that are immediately apparent to most LLM users, it's used to draw conclusions about LLM capabilities as a whole. It has a limitation sections, but it's not really used to inform the conclusion, which frames the work as a strong systemic assessment, despite the study providing very little signal on how any real, well-designed system will perform.
My main worry with things like these are that these studies get broad coverage, which will lead to us actively hindering quality-of-care because of extremely poorly ran experiments, when players like @SophontAI are doing incredible work at actually advancing medical AI capabilities with well-designed experiments and studies.
Quoting @rohanpaul_ai
This paper tests an LLM on real NHS (National Health Service) medication reviews and finds it spots risks but misses safe fixes.
They ran a medication safety reviewer on structured United Kingdom National Health Service (NHS) primary care records, mostly coded fields without typed notes, then had an expert clinician grade 277 sampled patients.
AI did not miss any case where an intervention (a clear action, like starting or stopping a drug) was needed, but it produced a fully correct review in only 46.9% of patients.
When it failed, the main issue was context, for example acting confident with missing details, applying guidelines (the usual best practice rules) without patient goals, or mixing up drug facts.
The paper argues this gap between spotting risk and choosing the right next step is why LLMs still need human checking in real clinics.
----
Paper Link – arxiv. org/abs/2512.21127
Paper Title: "A Real-World Evaluation of LLM Medication Safety Reviews in NHS Primary Care"

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
I'm personally very bearish on MUVERA due to its many, many, failure cases, but I have a lot of respect for the @weaviate_io folks, so I gave this another deep read to see if there were things that could change my mind.
However this has me a bit puzzled, if I'm reading the graph below right, it means that MUVERA itself produces a ~50+% incompressible performance degradation at commonly used indexing parameters, and still a ~20% degradation at near-bruteforce search tier parameters (ef=1024), meaning that the degradation would be purely due to MUVERA itself.
For most retrieval uses, this would make the method completely unusable, as this degradation for many workflows is almost similar to the one we'd experience from replacing semantic search with pure bm25/keyword search.
I feel like I'm missing something here so I'm very happy to be corrected if I'm misinterpreting the results!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HAYkmkbacAQm9Gh.png
Quoting @femke_plantinga
Multi-vector embeddings (ColBERT, ColPali) are budget killers.
But MUVERA can cut your memory footprint by 70%.
Multi-vector models offer incredible retrieval but suffer from massive memory overhead and slow indexing. MUVERA (Multi-Vector Retrieval via Fixed Dimensional Encodings) compresses these into single, fixed-dimensional vectors.
How it works:
MUVERA condenses a sequence of vectors (e.g., 100x96d) into one vector via:
1️⃣ Space Partitioning: Groups vectors into buckets using SimHash or k-means clustering.
2️⃣ Dimensionality Reduction: Applies random linear projection to compress each sub-vector while preserving dot products.
3️⃣ Repetitions: Repeats the process multiple times and concatenates results to improve accuracy.
4️⃣ Final Projection: Optional final compression (not used in Weaviate's implementation).
The impact (LoTTE benchmark):
- Memory: 12GB → <1GB.
- Indexing: 20+ mins → 3-6 mins.
- HNSW Graph: 99% smaller.
There’s a trade-off:
You trade a slight dip in raw recall for massive efficiency gains. However, by tuning the HNSW `ef` parameter (e.g., `ef=512`), you can recover 80-90%+ recall while keeping costs low.
When should you use MUVERA?
→ Large-scale production RAG
→ Systems where memory/infrastructure costs are the direct bottleneck
→ Use cases requiring fast indexing
MUVERA in @weaviate_io 1.31+ takes just a couple of lines of code. You can tune three parameters (k_sim, d_proj, r_reps) to balance memory usage and retrieval accuracy for your specific use case.
Read the full technical deep-dive here:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HATi6KGWsAA0eBv.jpg

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
Phew!
slapping a minimal SOTA search agent is quick, but cleaning takes way moooooooore time than I expected.
i’ve been working on turning pi-serini from a BrowseComp-only setup into a
reusable benchmarked search-agent workspace,
and it’s now at a first public milestone.
pi-serini v0.1.x supports prebuilt index-driven BM25 agentic search and evaluation for:
- BrowseComp-Plus
- MS MARCO v1 Passage (DL19, DL20)
- & guidelines of how to add your customized benchmarks
Includes:
- BM25-backed pi search extension
- shared and sharded BM25 launch modes
- retrieval eval, judge eval (reference-free or answer-grounded), summarization, and reporting
- reproducible benchmark manifests
next milestone (maybe?):
document ingestion via Anserini IndexCollection, so you can index your own documents easily
then maybe do more fun exps :)
Enjoy!

clean_title: Introducing FlashQLA: high-performance linear attention kernels
summary:
🚀 Introducing FlashQLA: high-performance linear attention kernels built on TileLang.
⚡ 2–3× forward speedup. 2× backward speedup.
💻 Purpose-built for agentic AI on your personal devices.
💡Key insights:
1. Gate-driven automatic intra-card CP.
2. Hardware-friendly algebraic reformulation.
3. TileLang fused warp-specialized kernels.
FlashQLA boosts SM utilization via automatic intra-device CP. The gains are especially pronounced for TP setups, small models, and long-context workloads.
Instead of fusing the entire GDN flow into a single kernel, we split it into two kernels optimized for CP and backward efficiency. At large batch sizes this incurs extra memory I/O overhead vs. a fully fused approach, but it delivers better real-world performance on edge devices and long-context workloads.
The backward pass was the hardest part: we built a 16-stage warp-specialized pipeline under extremely tight on-chip memory constraints, ultimately achieving 2×+ kernel-level speedups.
We hope this is useful to the community!🫶🫶
Learn more:

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
clean_title: Introducing single-stage sparse coding for efficient retrieval
summary:
Thanks for sharing our work @lateinteraction @sum!
The idea is extremely simple:
- multi-vector retrieval is so costly that it often needs k-means to categorize tokens first;
- k-means is essentially a top-1 sparse coding method (n-dim dense->1-dim cluster id), which means it loses a lot of information in the middle stage;
- if we need sparsity anyway, why dont we just do a 1-stage, e2e sparse coding (n-dim dense in, k-dim sparse out)? then it becomes single-stage sparse retrieval (SSR );
- thus, SSR with topk (k=32 by default) is strictly better than multi-stage ones from an information-theoretic perspective, since it avoids this top-1 lossy k-means bottleneck.
In fact, SSR is essentially a "CSR-v3", part of the "learned sparse retrieval" thread of work we explored in the last 2 years:
- CSR (ICML'25 oral): unsupervised SAE + contrastive learning is superior for efficient retrieval;
- CSR-v2 (ICLR'26): ultra-sparse CSR with k as small as 2/4, 4x more efficient than CSRv1;
- SSR (v3, ICML'26): introduces CSR to token-level, showing sparse embedding can outperform dense ones at multi-vector regimes as well.
We actually submitted a "v4" recently that further cultivates the nice properties of sparse embeddings. Stay tuned!
Links to these works in the 🧵
Quoting @lateinteraction
Late-interaction sparse retrieval? 😁
With neuron-level inverted indexing, on top of unsupervised sparse autoencoders. Works much better than directly training sparse retrievers.
Lots of cool ideas developed & composed in here. Thanks for the insights @Veritas2026 @yifeiwang77!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJhwBN3a4AAlSFD.png
clean_summary:
Thanks for sharing our work @lateinteraction @sum. The idea is that multi-vector retrieval is costly because it often relies on k-means clustering, which is a top-1 sparse coding method that loses information. Instead, we propose a one-stage, end-to-end sparse coding approach called single-stage sparse retrieval (SSR), which directly maps dense vectors to sparse codes, avoiding the information loss of k-means.

SSR with topk (default 32) is theoretically better than multi-stage methods because it preserves more information. This approach is part of a series of works on learned sparse retrieval, including CSR (unsupervised autoencoder with contrastive learning), CSR-v2 (ultra-sparse with k as small as 2 or 4), and CSR-v3 (token-level sparse embeddings outperforming dense ones). A recent v4 version further improves these properties. These methods have demonstrated significant efficiency and performance gains in retrieval tasks.
